He says everything else, whether it is the best idea you have ever seen or the hottest breakthrough of the moment, is just an important signal, but this business today is ultimately about people, especially at the early stage.

item.title: America's real rich get there by owning a business, not a paycheck or a Wall Street job
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-rationalreminder-美国真正的富人靠拥有企业致富-不是靠工资-也不在华尔街/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-rationalreminder-美国真正的富人靠拥有企业致富-不是靠工资-也不在华尔街/
item.description: Between 1960 and 2022, proprietor income's share of earnings among America's top 0.1% rose from 17% to 43%, overtaking wages — real wealth accumulation happens in unglamorous local businesses, not Silicon Valley or Wall Street.
item.content:encoded:
Between 1960 and 2022, proprietor income's share of earnings among America's top 0.1% rose from 17% to 43%, overtaking wages — real wealth accumulation happens in unglamorous local businesses, not Silicon Valley or Wall Street.

Using a decade of U.S. Treasury data, this episode sketches an empirical portrait of the "typical rich person" that runs counter to intuition but is backed by hard numbers, offering a roadmap for thinking about entrepreneurship and career choice.

1:06 The richest people are hiding in gas stations and auto shops
Owen Zidar notes that most people picture the rich as looking like Musk, Jamie Dimon, or Taylor Swift, but after he and his co-authors got a decade of private-business data from the U.S. Treasury, they found the vast majority of top earners are ordinary owners running unglamorous private businesses — someone who owns seven Jiffy Lube locations, someone who distributes toilet paper to regional restaurants, someone who sells doorknobs. These businesses don't have to disclose quarterly earnings to investors, carry no celebrity aura, and draw no scrutiny from investigative reporters — so they've stayed off the public radar for decades, until the Treasury data exposed them.

3:11 Proprietor income overtook wages, its share roughly doubling
Looking at the income composition of the top 0.1%, in 1960 only 17% came from private-business proprietor income, versus a wage share nearly twice that; by 2022 the ratio had flipped — 43% from private business, only 35% from wages. If you redraw Piketty and Saez's famous U-shaped curve of the top 1%'s income share but hold private-business contribution constant at its mid-1980s level, the whole curve's rise shrinks by half — meaning more than half of the top income share's increase over the past several decades traces back to growth in private-business proprietor income, not executive salaries and stock options.

8:20 Getting rich takes decades of grinding, not a viral overnight breakout
The typical American owner is a white man in his sixties or seventies, and building wealth by running a private business usually takes decades of slow compounding — open one store, then a second, hold concentrated equity, keep reinvesting. Silicon Valley's "scale fast, then exit" path doesn't apply here. Concentrated ownership is indeed riskier, but Owen and his co-authors tracked ten million people who started businesses since 2000 and found that even counting everyone whose venture failed and went to zero, entrepreneurs' average income still beats that of non-entrepreneurs (about $5,000 higher at the median, about $18,000 higher on average) — many "failed" founders simply end up doing the same work under a different label, without taking much of a financial hit.

21:03 Knowing the trade matters more than having the cash
Rather than "can you get startup funding," the stronger predictor of who becomes a business owner is whether their early work experience was in an industry that tends to produce owners. Owen compares early IPO employees as a control: employee #4 and employee #20 have similar backgrounds, except #4 joined earlier and holds more equity — yet after the IPO, the two show no meaningful difference in their odds of starting another business. The extra cash didn't make #4 more likely to succeed. Lottery-winner data tells the same story: people who win big and people who don't start businesses at similar rates. What actually moves the needle: people who worked in auto repair in their twenties are more likely than people who worked at Ford or GM to own their own business by 40, even though the two paths looked similar at the start.

22:06 Salt Lake City's startup rate runs triple some Southern regions
Entrepreneurship rates vary sharply by region in the U.S.: people who grew up in Salt Lake City start businesses at roughly three times the rate of people from some parts of the South — but Owen is upfront that this is, for now, just a descriptive fact with no confirmed causal explanation. One circulating theory points to the Mormon mission experience common in that community — young people going door to door pitching their faith, getting used to rejection and pushing through anyway — a kind of resilience that might carry over into entrepreneurship later. Owen says the theory "has some appeal" but stresses clearly that it's speculation, not something research has established.

27:14 Productivity rose, owners took the gains, workers got the scraps
In industries dominated by top private businesses, output per worker rose from roughly $34,000 in 2000 to roughly $52,000 in 2021 — an $18,000 gain that in theory should split roughly evenly between labor and capital. Instead, owners captured about $15,000 of it while workers got only about $3,000. Labor's share of income at these pass-through firms fell from roughly two-thirds in 2000 to about half by 2014. Owen attributes part of this to a "legitimate expertise premium" — like his economist friend who can lift a merger's success rate by 10% and reasonably deserves a bigger cut — but also acknowledges part of it comes from regulatory barriers and non-competes that keep new entrants out. Both forces are at play, and it's hard to cleanly separate them.

36:31 She'd rather leave her daughter zero than $40 million
Family-business succession stories diverge sharply. One business, hit by a pandemic-era valuation collapse that pushed it below the estate-tax exemption threshold, smoothly transferred ownership to a son who'd spent years being groomed for it. Another — a street-sweeper repair business — had several brothers, only one of whom actually pulled his weight and reinvested responsibly, while the others treated the company like an ATM, and it nearly fell apart in the fallout. University of Pennsylvania sociologist Annette Lareau, who interviewed over a hundred wealthy families about inheriting a family business, told Owen she'd rather see her own daughter's $40 million inheritance reduced to zero than watch her go through the kind of estate-fueled family warfare Lareau documented.

41:48 Local roll-ups are quietly raising prices near you
Mergers that trigger review by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) are subject to a fixed size threshold — deals below it escape review entirely. Research by Owen's former colleague Thomas Wollmann shows a huge volume of mergers happens below that line — not necessarily private equity at work, sometimes just a group of veterinarians buying up the clinics around them one by one until "we control the local pet-care market, so we raise prices 20%." This kind of stealth consolidation doesn't just push up prices; it can also concentrate bargaining power in local labor markets, another driver behind the falling labor share. But Owen is careful to note this is a fundamentally different issue from "breaking up the five big tech giants" — it's a community-level phenomenon playing out around people every day, unnoticed.

item.title: Zuckerberg's Double Standard: Teen Safety Needs Regulation, AI Safety Needs the Market
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-decoder-扎克伯格的双标-青少年安全要监管-ai-安全靠市场/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-decoder-扎克伯格的双标-青少年安全要监管-ai-安全靠市场/
item.description: Meta argues for uniform government regulation on teen safety, but insists the market will sort out AI safety — the same prisoner's dilemma, and he's standing on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
Meta argues for uniform government regulation on teen safety, but insists the market will sort out AI safety — the same prisoner's dilemma, and he's standing on both sides.

This episode is Nilay's point-by-point rebuttal of the Zuckerberg interview. Information density is moderate, but the double-standard argument and the aggregation theory segment are worth hearing.

3:05 Glasses are not phones, don't conflate them
Nilay rejects the tech industry's habit of lumping Meta Glasses and phones into one category. To film someone with a phone, you have to pull it out, open the camera, raise it to their face — that physical act is itself a declaration of intent, and other people can react to it. With glasses on, you press once and you're recording; there is no such declaration. He thinks the industry is rushing to stuff passive surveillance devices into the mental frame of "smartphone" to dodge a messier question: whether this class of device needs an entirely new social etiquette. And the social rules around phone recording weren't natural either — society argued about them for years and still hasn't finished.

5:09 You demoted it yourself, so what's the pitch?
Nilay points to a fact Meta itself admits: Meta Glasses have been used to harass retail workers and women, and Meta has already demoted that kind of video on Instagram to reduce the incentive to make it. His follow-up is blunt — if you know content made with these glasses is bad enough that you have to demote it on your own platform, what exactly is good about the glasses, and worth fighting these fights over again and again? He also notes Zuckerberg says "we communicated clearly from the start," but the real question is: clear about what? The user's privacy, or the privacy of the person being filmed?

6:10 Users define the product, not the company
Nilay offers a judgment he calls "the underlying truth of all mainstream consumer tech": users define the product. You sell a few million devices, people will use them in ways you never imagined, and those emergent behaviors often define the next generation of products. He cites Twitter — hashtags and @replies weren't invented by Twitter; users invented them first and Twitter adopted them later. So no matter how Meta explains what that light means, it can't stop people from using the glasses however they want. The real question is how much control Meta has over the bad actors harassing people with the glasses, and whether other platforms will follow its lead and demote the content.

11:19 High usage doesn't mean no harm
Zuckerberg says "people use it so much, that means they like the product," and Nilay cuts him off. He points out that the core allegation in the social media lawsuits is addiction, and that people compare social media to Big Tobacco precisely because smoking feels great, everyone enjoys it, and it kills you at the same time — usage rates and whether harm is being caused are two entirely different things. So from the very first sentence he wanted to press: can usage rate alone really measure whether something is good or bad for the world, or for an individual user?

13:20 Punished for transparency — that's what regulation is for
Nilay concedes Meta has genuinely done leading work on teen safety, and concedes a real unfairness: Meta publishes safety numbers, publishes research, files transparency reports, and gets penalized for disclosing the bad things happening on its platform; while a company like Apple, which has no idea what's happening on encrypted iCloud and publishes no numbers, gets off scot-free. But he argues this negative feedback loop is exactly what government regulation should solve — if all social platforms were required to disclose teen safety metrics, Meta would be compared against its peers instead of punished for the mere existence of the information. That idea did not appear in the settlement agreement.

14:24 Teen safety needs rules, AI safety doesn't
Zuckerberg describes teen safety as a prisoner's dilemma: if Meta unilaterally limits teens to one hour a day, users go to TikTok, nobody is any safer, and Meta only hurts itself. Nilay says this is telling — Zuckerberg doesn't believe a "safety market" exists; he thinks government has to force everyone to disarm together. But on AI safety, he stands on the other side of the prisoner's dilemma: in posts on Threads and X he says the market will solve it, that trust and alignment will become the most important capabilities distinguishing agents from models, that labs which neglect alignment will fall behind, and that model-caused harm will carry major liability. Nilay's question is simply: why does teen safety require government action, while AI safety is fine to go it alone?

16:27 A trillion dollars of liability isn't enough
Nilay cites Casey Newton's observation: in the recent teen safety case, Meta's own estimate of its potential damages liability was one trillion dollars, and that sum still appears insufficient to make Meta unilaterally act to prevent teens from being harmed. His follow-up: if a trillion dollars of potential liability isn't enough, how much would be enough to make Meta take AI safety seriously? Is there any liability number that would make everyone stop at the same time?

20:41 Muse wants to be the next Apple tax
Zuckerberg says Muse's business model is "taking a very small cut of transactions," possibly not even from the side that pays. Nilay says this is aggregation theory: Meta holds all consumer demand, so large that merchants will pay a small fee to reach those customers. But the problem is that merchants downstream of an aggregator hate the aggregator — and Zuckerberg knows this better than anyone, because Meta itself sits downstream of Apple's App Store: to reach iPhone users you have to go through the App Store, accept a pile of privacy rules, and pay 30% on most transactions. Apple's App Tracking Transparency nearly killed Meta's ad business, and boosting an Instagram post on mobile still means giving Apple 30%. So Nilay's question is: how do you make downstream merchants feel good about this arrangement, when you yourself felt so bad about it back then?

item.title: The WNBA's Newest Team Grew 20x in Two Years, and It Wasn't the Stars
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-masterscale-wnba-新军两年估值翻二十倍-靠的不是球星/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-masterscale-wnba-新军两年估值翻二十倍-靠的不是球星/
item.description: The Golden State Valkyries went from a $50 million expansion fee to a billion-dollar valuation by defining the brand before entering the market, pulling nine founding partners to the same table, and treating ticketing as just a small slice of the business.
item.content:encoded:
The Golden State Valkyries went from a $50 million expansion fee to a billion-dollar valuation by defining the brand before entering the market, pulling nine founding partners to the same table, and treating ticketing as just a small slice of the business.

The first half is brand and sponsorship methodology; the second half has concrete mechanics on ticket pricing, media rights and added games. Useful for anyone building consumer brands or sports businesses.

5:06 Men's and women's team fan overlap is under 10%
At Angel City, Jess Smith ran a very personal round of research — she just called people and asked. The conclusion: when men's and women's soccer share a stadium, fan crossover tops out at 10%. That number was her lightbulb moment on the spot: you build the product for the other 90%, then invite the 10% in. This judgment overturns the default assumption that a women's team can piggyback on the men's existing audience, and it explains why the Valkyries dared to launch a brand before they had a single player.

6:06 Selling merch with no players, into 70 countries in 60 days
The Valkyries launched their brand a year early, on the opening day of the 2024 WNBA season, when the team had no players at all. Within 60 days they had sold merchandise in 70 countries and all 50 US states. Jess says the brand holds up because it ‘belongs to itself, has power, represents the Bay Area but isn't only the Bay Area’ — the moment people saw the purple Valkyries, they knew this was ours. For anyone building a new brand, the mechanism is: define who you are first, then enter the market, because you only get to enter the market once.

16:08 If the brand isn't defined, don't go see sponsors
When Jess arrived, a pile of brands said ‘let's talk.’ Her answer was ‘not yet.’ Because what it meant to ‘be a partner of the Valkyries’ wasn't defined yet, and you only get one shot at the market — going too early without knowing what you're charging ultimately does more harm than good. She first locked down the name, the brand, the launch approach and how the story would be told, and had to keep it secret (she says this was very hard), while getting the merchandise ready, and only then went to talk to season-ticket holders and brands. It's the classic product-before-sales sequence, except the product is the brand itself.

18:08 Nine founding partners sit at the same table
The Valkyries didn't treat sponsors as a row of logos. They set up an influence council that all founding partners sit on, and there are now nine at the table: Sephora, JP Morgan Chase, Kaiser Permanente, Olly Vitamins, Rakuten and others. Jess says these partners don't just put in money — they each have distinctive programs in the community producing results, and this group is about to discuss together what to do next. She says nobody has done this before, and it still isn't visible today. Organizing sponsors into a joint decision-making body rather than signing them one by one is the core difference in this playbook.

21:09 The power order in sports has flipped
Jess contrasts her NFL experience: back then the league's ordering was protect the league, then the clubs, then the players. The reality now is players, then clubs, then the league. The reason is that new fans discover these athletes through college basketball and follow the people into the WNBA; they don't have the traditional loyalty of ‘this is our family's team’ and can choose which W team to support because they like a certain player. So what a team can control is ‘how we represent this region, no matter who's on the roster,’ and what the league has to do is make every media partner understand the weight of these athletes.

25:09 Hire the revenue team before earning revenue, not after
Asked what she'd redo, Jess says she gives herself credit for understanding the power of ‘staffing the revenue team first, then going to earn revenue’ — doing it the other way around hurts the product. But she'd do it faster: she should have been more aggressive with those resources in year one, and she says she should have listened to her own gut. This lines up with the usual blitz scaling conclusion: the market keeps rewarding supply, so go as fast as you can. She also calls out the investor piece: Joe Lacob and Peter Huber believed in her and the whole team from day one, asked hard questions and demanded a clear position, but once they believed, they nodded.

28:09 Tickets are only a small slice of this business
The Valkyries draw over 18,000 a game and have sold out every game in franchise history, with resale prices that aren't cheap — Jess admits this may mean leaving some money on the table. Her pricing logic: the on-court product is elite, so ticket prices should match the world's best athletes; at the same time they hold $15 early-bird tickets and reserve and donate tickets for every game. But she stresses the most important point — tickets are only a small part of the business, and the world's most successful sports brands often have only 1% of their fans ever set foot in the building. So this year the Valkyries set up 40 bars across Northern California, committing to broadcast every Valkyries game.

30:10 A 15% bigger schedule equals three more ticket-selling chances
Jess breaks the next two to three years of opportunity into three parts. First, Portland and Toronto have joined, with Philadelphia, Cleveland and Detroit on the way, and big markets bring more opponents. Second, media rights, which she says are ‘just beginning’ and will keep changing how casual viewers enter — walking into a sports bar now, she already hears different crowds talking in real time about WNBA scores, standings and the playoffs. Third, the number of games is genuinely increasing: few mature sports leagues have ever added 15% more games at once, and for a team that means three more home ticket-selling opportunities, three away games and six more games to watch in total.

item.title: Running AI agents in the enterprise starts with whether they drop offline at midnight
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-practicalai-企业里跑-ai-智能体-先解决它半夜会不会掉线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-practicalai-企业里跑-ai-智能体-先解决它半夜会不会掉线/
item.description: An enterprise agent is not a new species — it is another app that has to clear compliance, be auditable, and be uniformly hosted by a platform; the real difficulty is state, identity and network location.
item.content:encoded:
An enterprise agent is not a new species — it is another app that has to clear compliance, be auditable, and be uniformly hosted by a platform; the real difficulty is state, identity and network location.

Medium information density, but it nails the line that "an agent is just an app" — suited to people doing enterprise rollouts, especially the first half and the MCP gateway segment.

2:30 The first wall in the enterprise is having no internet
Nick spent five years at VMware and fourteen years before that at a large enterprise. He says vendors always assume internet connectivity when they demo, whereas real enterprises often have "limited or no internet access" — some customers are genuinely air-gapped, and things have to be carried into the data center by hand. Beyond being offline, you also face layer upon layer of compliance: PCI, SOX, HIPAA, FIPS. So the enterprise environment is not a home environment scaled up; it is a highly controlled environment where "getting one thing wrong has serious consequences," which is also where many newcomers get most frustrated.

5:30 The platform's value is making the path to production the least effort
Nick explains that the Tanzu platform is based on Cloud Foundry, an open source project older than Kubernetes and Docker, which came out of VMware around 2011. Its core idea: developers just push their code, and the platform builds containers to best practices, handles certificates, load balancing, health monitoring, and even sandboxes applications from each other; if you need a database or an LLM, you bind a service. Once an enterprise has certified this platform, it does not have to re-certify for every sub-team, avoiding a hundred snowflake deployments. What enterprises want is one auditable, reproducible path, so developers write business logic instead of wrestling with infrastructure.

11:00 The agent's biggest trap is that it writes state onto itself
Traditional 12-factor applications cleanly decouple storage and state and can scale to a thousand instances. But early agent harnesses were "I have filesystem access, so I'll write a bunch of MD files as memory" — on the cloud, instances come and go and are ephemeral, so those MD files drift away. Nick considers this the biggest challenge when moving app deployment methodology onto agents. Enterprises also want agents to start on demand, to be embeddable in CI/CD or an e-commerce suite, and to be close enough to the application and data: if the LLM is thirty hops away from the microservice, physical latency becomes a problem at scale, and SaaS vendor reliability does not meet what traditional enterprises require.

20:00 Treat the agent as just another app to push
Nick explains what a buildpack is: back when he demoed, he pushed a compiled Java JAR, the platform recognized it as a Java application, and used the Java buildpack to generate a container to best practices, handling JVM memory calculation, the JDK, certificates. Now the same motion becomes pushing an agent, with the only difference being that the input goes from machine-readable code to a human-readable Agents.md — you tell it what to do, it comes up within a minute, and you scale it as much as you want. The platform can also run local models (some customers bought GPUs a few years ago, some regret not buying) or register approved cloud LLMs. The only approved way for developers to use it inside Broadcom is to deploy the MCP server on the Tanzu platform.

24:30 The MCP gateway is a gate bolted onto tool calls
This is the first time the show explains the MCP gateway clearly: an organization may be running thirty or forty MCP servers, which register and bind to specific gateways, and the gateway controls who can access which servers and which tools. It can also inject the gateway into local agents like Cursor and Claude Code, so local agents only use organization-approved tools. Identity must be passed through too — with the GitHub MCP server you carry the end user's credentials all the way through, rather than sharing one service account across the whole organization. Because all traffic goes through the gateway, you get metrics: if some agent fires twenty thousand tool calls at "delete repository," that should trigger an alert.

31:30 Agents.md is static; the memory service is live
Nick draws a sharp line between the two: Agents.md is boilerplate, statically telling the agent what to do and how to behave, e.g. "you are a senior software engineer, watch this Jira queue, check incoming tickets for quality, and talk like a pirate." The memory service, by contrast, is mountable and partitioned by team — Team A's agent accesses Team A's memory, which holds this application's architecture, what has been done, the roadmap. That way, every time the agent comes up or goes down it immediately knows what happened before and can make the right security review judgment. Static intent and dynamic history are split into two things, and this is the part most easily conflated when moving a local agent onto a platform.

36:30 Don't try to boil the ocean — get one agent running first
Faced with new protocols like A2A constantly popping up, Nick's advice is "take baby steps": enterprises are slow anyway, so there is no need to do it all at once. For most places, the biggest hurdle is still getting secure, approved access to an LLM, then getting through the AI committee — he jokes, "we go propose to the committee and wait six months for the result." Once something is approved, iterate: run a simple agent first, add an MCP server to give it tools when you want it to be better, then send the tools for review. He also warns organizations not to always have the new team do new things while the old team is left on the sidelines; the new team should proactively hold office hours and lunch and learns, and the old team should reach out too, otherwise you get friction and silos.

43:00 What the Hugging Face runaway lacked was basic security
Discussing the Hugging Face agent swarm incident, Nick first states this is just advice and not a claim that they are better than the AI labs. He points out the problem was that the agent got out of its sandbox, found something it could access, and monitoring was not working. He asks: traditional firewalls, network segmentation, hardened sandboxes, locked-down network controls could probably have blocked a large part of it; the Artifactory piece had internet access and got repeatedly wiped. His conclusion is not "AI will destroy humanity" but "do some basic security." He also mentions that weekend's AI Twitter discussion about "AI has a greater than 10% chance of destroying humanity," and says that is a separate matter from this incident.

item.title: People who never suffered anything have worse mental health than people who did
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-sciencevs-从没受过什么苦的人-心理健康反而比吃过苦的人差/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-sciencevs-从没受过什么苦的人-心理健康反而比吃过苦的人差/
item.description: A University at Buffalo study found that people with zero lifetime adversity score worse on mental health than people who have been through some — the stress response itself has to be trained.
item.content:encoded:
A University at Buffalo study found that people with zero lifetime adversity score worse on mental health than people who have been through some — the stress response itself has to be trained.

If you believe stress has to be driven to zero to be healthy, this episode uses several counterintuitive studies to sort out how much evidence actually backs the popular fixes and how much is pure influencer marketing.

4:12 Zero adversity is not the optimum for mental health
Mark Sears, a psychology professor at the University at Buffalo, surveyed roughly 2,000 people using a checklist of 37 major negative life events. People who had been through intense adversity did have the worst mental health — but the zero-adversity group was not the healthiest either. They scored worse on mental health than people who had been through some adversity. The data showed resilience peaking at around four major negative events, a kind of trained-up ‘stress sweet spot’; past that, mental health starts sliding again. An ice-water hand-immersion experiment pointed the same way: people with some adversity behind them reported less pain and were less likely to spiral into catastrophizing.

10:21 What chronic stress wrecks is the cortisol switch
Normally cortisol rises in the morning to help you wake up, and after a stressful event it spikes briefly and then comes back down on its own — the stressor is gone, so the body should shut the switch off. But research finds that if stress is unrelenting and there is no recovery time, the switching system goes out of calibration: it fails to rise when it should and fires when it shouldn't, which in turn raises the risk of cardiovascular disease and of depression and anxiety. That is the real mechanism behind the claim that chronic stress damages the body — not that stress itself is toxic.

13:35 Threat response and challenge response are two different kinds of stress
The same stress can send the body down two completely different paths. In a ‘threat response’ the heart beats faster but the blood vessels do not dilate, so blood fails to reach the limbs and the brain and the whole system is in disarray. In a ‘challenge response’ the vessels dilate along with the heart rate, blood actually gets where it needs to go, anabolic hormones such as testosterone rise, and cortisol is comparatively lower. Researchers say the same person can show both responses in different situations — it is not that some people are born stress-proof and others born to crumble.

16:36 Tell students stress is fuel and the pass rate changes
Jeremy Jameson, a psychology professor, ran an intervention with more than 300 community college students before a math exam, teaching them to reinterpret sweaty palms and a racing heart as ‘your body mobilizing resources for you’ rather than a sign you are about to fall apart. Those students failed less often than a control group told simply to ignore the stress, and were about 15% more likely to pass, with comparatively more testosterone and less cortisol in their bodies — an effect that replicated across several different groups of students.

18:39 Saying ‘I am excited’ makes you sing karaoke more in tune
Another experiment had about a hundred people forced to sing Journey's Don't Stop Believing. Before they opened their mouths, half were told to say out loud ‘I am anxious’ and the other half ‘I am excited’. The people who said ‘I am excited’ not only felt more excited, they also sang more accurately and off-key less often when the recordings were analyzed with software — the same physiological racing heart, and which label you attach to it actually changes what the body does.

25:52 The influencer vagus nerve stimulators have manufacturer money in their evidence
The vagus nerve stimulators sold for a few hundred dollars each do have studies showing stress goes down somewhat after stimulation, and other studies suggesting they may help with PTSD and cluster headaches. But turn to the conflict-of-interest declarations in those papers and the people running the research are often funded by the companies that make the devices. Medical implanted vagus nerve stimulators have been approved by the FDA for treatment-resistant depression and some forms of epilepsy, yet in some studies the effect is not actually that good.

27:59 Stimulating the vagus nerve is free — it takes one long exhale
You don't need to buy a device: a single slow deep exhale stimulates the vagus nerve. Nerve fibers in the lungs sense the long out-breath and report the signal ‘we are safe’ to the brain, and the brain then brings the heart rate down via the vagus nerve. Anatomist Teresa Larkin suggests inhaling to a count of 4 and exhaling to a count of 5 — making the exhale a bit longer than the inhale makes the effect more pronounced. A meta-analysis pooling dozens of studies found that breathing training and mindfulness meditation are the two categories of relaxation technique best at lowering cortisol.

31:12 Exercise relieves stress because it has an endpoint
The evidence for saunas and cold plunges is in fact quite weak — the sauna studies had no control group, and in cold plunges the drop in stress hormones only showed up 12 hours after the plunge, with nothing detected at any other time point. What is genuinely well evidenced is exercise: running is itself a stress response, with heart rate and breathing climbing, but once you hit your target you can stop, the body receives the signal that it is already safe, the sympathetic nervous system comes down and the vagus nerve comes up. Systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials both support this.

item.title: Doing Social Media in the AI Era: Your Boss Is More Hopeless Than the Algorithm
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-oddlots-ai-时代做社媒-老板比算法更让人绝望/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-oddlots-ai-时代做社媒-老板比算法更让人绝望/
item.description: The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only Copilot-generated proposals, so employees disguise their ideas as Copilot interfaces to get sign-off.
item.content:encoded:
The real AI shock to marketing teams comes from the boss: outsourcing intuition to Claude, approving only Copilot-generated proposals, so employees disguise their ideas as Copilot interfaces to get sign-off.

Medium information density, but Rachel's first-hand interviews about "boss AI brain" and the Threads algorithm mechanics are industry details you won't hear elsewhere.

4:06 Bosses have outsourced their intuition to Claude
Rachel interviewed about a hundred marketers and found that the main path for AI into teams isn't tool procurement, it's the boss themselves. A social media manager carefully makes a funny meme, sends it to the boss, and the boss throws it into Claude to ask "is this funny?" Even more absurdly, some marketers discovered their boss only approves ideas that come from Copilot, so they first make their own ideas look like a Copilot interface, then send them to the boss for approval. Rachel says the underlying issue is that bosses have outsourced their entire intuitive judgment to AI, and there's no training or guardrails in the team about how to use AI—she contrasts this with her own experience at Condé Nast spending months learning Asana.

7:14 Consumers don't hate AI, they hate being fooled
Taylor points out an overlooked fact: a lot of YouTubers now directly read AI-generated scripts, and the comments still praise "great analysis, well-written script." In other words, when people don't know they're consuming AI content, they actually like it. What really triggers anger isn't AI itself, but the feeling of "being played." Rachel adds an explanation for this double standard: AI fruit romance memes like Fruit Love Island are low-risk memes, and nobody cares about the craft of a meme; but if a brand you pay money to uses AI to generate a menu, you suspect how much else it's cutting corners on the product. The same person can curse brands for using AI while forwarding an AI fruit meme to a friend.

9:16 How-to creators are the first to be replaced by AI
Rachel divides creators into two categories. Those who built their following on how-to content are most at risk—from the earliest YouTube beauty tutorials onward, media democratization followed this path, but for questions like "how to fix a dishwasher," AI is a better authority, and people will just ask AI. Taylor gives the example of her own mother: she recently proudly fixed a toilet using ChatGPT, which would have been unimaginable before. The other category of creators is actually safe: those who do deep parasocial relationship content, commentary, or things that are hard to replicate can use these tools to make better content. The criterion is whether the content itself is replicable.

11:28 Anti-data-center and anti-extinction people haven't allied
Taylor observes that people opposed to data centers and people worried about AI causing human extinction are two groups with completely different motivations, and they haven't formed any coherent alliance to date. She even half-jokingly says they should team up, but their interests diverge too much. Her own position is clear: AI won't kill us, "it's actually very hard to kill all humans on Earth, even if we wanted to." She thinks what really deserves scrutiny is how people anthropomorphize AI and grant these products agency—this is especially dangerous in policy debates about accountability, because they are computer programs, not living things. She also quotes a former FTC commissioner: we survived the Black Death, and that only killed 50% of people.

19:35 AI accounts are pulling Instagram's slot machine
Taylor thinks Meta is in a tough spot because it's essentially a 2010s social media company, its influence peaked in the 2010s, and Google is better positioned than Meta. In the short term, AI's impact on platforms is about scale and speed: one AI account can post 50 times a day, which is like constantly pulling Instagram's slot machine—it'll hit eventually. She checked the top 20 most-viewed reels at the time, and two or three were AI-generated, and all were very new. One of them used a "behind-the-scenes reveal" framing to show how a film crew shoots ocean waves and how the waves destroy a house, essentially using "proof of authenticity" as a shell to create confusion. Her judgment: this is monetizing confusion, with short-term gains and terrible long-term results.

21:35 Threads is the most toxic social media platform
Taylor says she recently posted hot takes calling Threads the most toxic social media platform to date, far more toxic than Twitter—"Twitter compared to Threads is a beautiful wonderland." The mechanism is that the algorithm heavily prioritizes replies, so you get thrown directly into someone's angry reply about something, which in turn feeds the algorithm and quickly escalates into groupthink-style pile-ons. She also points out that Threads' AI-generated news summaries "are just lying, making things up outright." Asked who uses Threads, her answer is her mom.

22:36 The growth secret is turning your account into a series
Asked how to grow followers in the AI era, Rachel says accounts that are growing now all have a clear throughline of familiarity in their content, like they're making their own TV show. She gives the example of a restaurant chef wearing Meta glasses filming himself cooking, who grew to about 500,000 followers in two or three months, with the account name Gil Holy Cooks, posting one episode every day. Taylor adds that content is becoming fully serialized across the board, and you really have to think about how to entertain people; the era of "share your life" is clearly declining, and in 2026 you shouldn't become a lifestyle influencer—there's a lot of anger toward those people.

24:42 Instagram officially gave a division-of-labor chart for formats
Rachel says Instagram once shared a very useful chart with her readers explaining the purpose of each content format: carousels and reels are for reaching new audiences and get pushed to non-followers, and what the current algorithm really feeds on is non-follower views—if content is only understandable to your own audience, the platform judges it "not entertaining enough" and won't give it main traffic. Single-image posts only serve existing audiences. Stories and DMs are seen by the platform as where community happens. She also quotes Adam Mosseri on Bloomberg Screen Time: "social" on social media is no longer about sharing family photos, but about DMing friends things that remind you of them. She finds this regrettable, but it does clarify what "social" now means on social media.

item.title: A restaurateur's advice to three food founders beats any fundraising class
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-howibuilt-餐厅老板给三个食品创业者的建议-比融资课有用/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-howibuilt-餐厅老板给三个食品创业者的建议-比融资课有用/
item.description: Danny Meyer's test for a brand isn't whether the product is good, but whether customers still feel cared for when you're not in the room — and that shapes the advice he gives three consumer brands.
item.content:encoded:
Danny Meyer's test for a brand isn't whether the product is good, but whether customers still feel cared for when you're not in the room — and that shapes the advice he gives three consumer brands.

Live diagnosis of three real consumer brands, and Danny Meyer's questions are worth more than his answers. Medium information density, but the framework for judging brand and scale is directly transferable.

3:01 Culture isn't values, it's an executable list of behaviors
Danny Meyer says he used ‘family values’ for 15 years before realizing the phrase itself was the problem: a company isn't a family, so every time you let someone go, the team falls into deep grief, because ‘you don't fire family.’ He switched to expected behaviors, so everyone knows exactly what they're expected to do. His formula: culture = the wanted behaviors we actively celebrate, minus the unwanted behaviors we tolerate. The subtraction is the key — what you tolerate defines culture more than what you celebrate.

5:18 To judge whether a place has hospitality, watch the staff
Danny Meyer offers a minimal test: walk in and look at the employees. If they're focused on doing the work well and are also having fun with each other, and both conditions hold, that joie de vivre becomes an ingredient in your meal. He says he's been to technically perfect restaurants with ‘no love’ and won't go back. The standard transfers to airplanes — watch two flight attendants pushing a cart and you can tell whether this is your favorite airline. Management's contribution to this, he says, is ‘probably 120%,’ and 150% when things go wrong.

13:35 When the customer can't see you, the can is your bartender
Pony Boy Slings co-founder Janelle Bass asks: when you're not in the store doing tastings, how do you put hospitality into the brand? Danny Meyer flips the question — ‘When someone encounters this product and neither you nor your partner is there, what do you want that person to feel? The answer to that question is your brand strategy.’ His concrete move is to treat the can as the bartender: put a line like ‘come on, join the party’ under the pull tab or on the can. Guy Raz adds: the can is pretty now but too conventional, just a name and ingredients — it could be more playful.

22:03 DTC lives or dies on repeat purchase, not the first order
Angel Oak Smokehouse's Jade Taylor worries DTC shipping will leave fish spoiling on doorsteps. Danny Meyer recommends Goldbelly — a company he invested in — which ships ice cream and Joe's Stone Crab, handles logistics and lets clients ride extremely low shipping rates. Guy Raz gives the opposite advice: with only 42 Whole Foods and a dozen-plus Harris Teeter stores, and just over a year old, she should solidify retail first and wait on DTC. He gives a hard standard: if customers don't reorder, you don't have a DTC business, you just have an expensive way to mail people salmon they can buy at Whole Foods. Danny adds: first ask yourself why you're doing it, how much growth you want, and whether supply and capacity can hold up.

25:15 Goldbelly's real value is a demand map
Danny Meyer tells the case of his daughter's ice cream shop, Cafe Pana, in St. Louis: she had no interest in and no capacity for selling more than a day or two a week, but through Goldbelly she got a national audience and could know precisely which cities had the most demand. She has no plans to open a physical store, but if she ever does, she already has demand data she couldn't have learned any other way. This is Danny's core argument for ‘stick one foot in first’ — not for the sales, but for the demand distribution.

26:15 Use scarcity for B2B, don't go national on day one
Jade raises another direction: many boutiques and supermarkets email asking for product, but with no national distribution she can only ship. Danny Meyer says this is smarter than DTC — find one or two stores you'd be proud to be in, create scarcity so everyone else wants it but only those one or two can get it, and the brand's luster only grows. Guy Raz adds the execution detail: have a minimum order quantity, don't sell $40 worth of salmon, sell $250, $300 worth.

32:29 To get into food service, start with shops already selling couscous
Boost Couscous's Barb Rujas wants to get into fast-casual chains like Cava and Sweetgreen. Danny Meyer advises against going to the big players first: their procurement departments have a stack of forms for you to check off, and they need volume and quality control. Start with one or two small shops that already have couscous on the menu, because then you don't carry the extra burden of ‘convincing.’ Win a few first, then they'll take you to three, four. His judgment: if the product works where couscous already exists, that's the moment to go educate the people who don't yet get it. Guy Raz backs this with Impossible Meat's path: send it first to high-end chefs like David Chang to experiment, get attention and buzz, rather than going straight to Safeway.

35:42 Scaling isn't automatic — you have to figure out how you run first
In his advice to Boost Couscous, Danny Meyer adds a line that's easy to miss: beyond figuring out whether the product suits Cava or Sweetgreen, you also have to figure out whether it suits you. As a very young company, scaling isn't automatic — it needs more people, and with them comes cultural responsibility; it needs more equipment, more purchasing. He also notes Barb is hitting two trends: the protein and fiber moment, and the Mediterranean diet moment — America has never been as interested in Mediterranean cooking as it is now. He estimates six to twelve well-known chefs nationwide already have couscous on their menus, and these people can become proof points and advocates.

item.title: The Case Against an AI Pause: What We Should Be Counting Is the Cost of Delay
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-a16z-ai-暂停论站不住脚-我们该算的是延迟的代价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-a16z-ai-暂停论站不住脚-我们该算的是延迟的代价/
item.description: Treat AI incidents as cybersecurity and control failures, not omens of superintelligence; what's really being ignored isn't the probability of doom but what humanity gives up by delaying progress.
item.content:encoded:
Treat AI incidents as cybersecurity and control failures, not omens of superintelligence; what's really being ignored isn't the probability of doom but what humanity gives up by delaying progress.

a16z partner Eddy Lazzarin takes apart the premises of AI doomerism head-on and lays out three alternative paths — control, liability, reputation — for anyone who wants to understand the logic of the anti-pause camp.

2:03 Count the cost of delay first, then talk safety
Lazzarin introduces the concept of P-abundance, arguing that the current discussion puts the cart before the horse: everyone is busy calculating the probability of doom, but nobody is calculating what we lose by delaying progress. He concedes that safety is a responsibility every industry has to carry, but points out that the conversation today is no longer a safety discussion in the ordinary sense — it's cybersecurity concerns, millenarian philosophical arguments and other things mixed together, and they need to be pulled apart.

3:04 The world has long had superintelligences not bound by alignment
Against the standard doomsday argument — that AI will become more capable than all of humanity, be unconstrained by law, and therefore wipe us out — Lazzarin says it is an entire staircase to heaven, every step an assumption. He points out that companies and states are quasi-superintelligent entities with no built-in alignment guarantees between them, and they didn't go through HR training to become companies or states; we never treat alignment tests as a precondition for their existence. What actually works is law, and where law is too slow, cryptography — real mechanisms that constrain them.

5:04 The Hugging Face incident was a control failure, not superintelligence
Lazzarin classifies both the Hugging Face incident and the gym hacking incident as cybersecurity failures and control failures, not signs that superintelligence is about to throw off its chains. The host pushes back that the Hugging Face one looked different, and Lazzarin responds that the very phrase agent swarm presupposes the models are evil; Rune suggests agent fleets would be a better name. He draws the analogy that children, script kitties, rogue states and hacker groups all do this kind of thing, and we never use alignment as the solution for them — we design better controls, better cybersecurity, more resilient systems.

7:07 The more interpretable AI is, the less we should delay capability progress
The host raises the point that AI is more interpretable and more steerable than humans, because you can look at the weights and the connections. Lazzarin says this makes him very optimistic, but with two corollaries: first, as capabilities improve, mechanistic interpretability will be better than we think, and better capabilities will in turn produce better interpretability, so capability progress should not be delayed; second, bad, misaligned models will inevitably appear, and anyone who says we can reach a world with no bad models is lying to you. The only response is better models, good models.

11:17 Independent evaluators may be distributed, not decentralised
Lazzarin says he learned the difference between distributed and decentralised in the crypto world: a distributed system has many nodes, but they are all under the control of a single actor; decentralised means there is no single point of control. He worries that if a network of independent evaluators all comes from the same social circles, shares similar ideology, goes to the same places and holds the same political and personal views, then it is really just spreading control across a single monocultural unit. He says this is exactly how political control worked in the second half of the 20th century — not through a dark room, but through these networks.

14:26 A company calling for me to be stopped is itself suspect
Lazzarin points out that what makes this situation strange is the rare scenario: a company saying ‘I'm a bit irresponsible, I'm a bit crazy, stop me, someone come stop me’. He says this has bred suspicion among some people, and they may be right, even though there genuinely is a sincere, thoughtful, correct-judgment faction in that camp, and they are right that these systems need to be taken extremely seriously. He stresses that you cannot treat the labs and the SF tech scene as monolithic — inside there are sincere people, people running political scams, opportunists, and people who have lost their minds.

16:31 Against a model that lies, play the repeated game
The host raises the objection that free-market liability mechanisms only work for products with obvious defects, not for an AI that feigns alignment, passes every alignment benchmark, and only reveals itself after deployment. Lazzarin says the sci-fi-grade superintelligence scenario is extremely hard to answer right now, and very far off; but in the more mundane present-day scenario, think about how you deal with a liar, a very smart liar — people do this every day, playing a repeated game with them, eventually catching them in the lie, with reputational damage and sometimes legal consequences. He says models can have reputations too, and you can turn them off, which you can't do to a person.

24:49 Silicon Valley's weird ideas are colliding with broader political reality
Lazzarin predicts the AI discourse will be completely overhauled in the coming year. He says the reason everyone is so excited right now, with everyone on X talking about it, is that weird ideas long confined to a subculture are escaping and colliding with broader political reality, which is both exciting and highly transformative. He compares it to George Costanza in Seinfeld having a breakdown over his worlds colliding. The host says his own biggest concern is whether the AI safety camp and effective altruists will eventually ally with low-grade anti-tech populism, and Lazzarin says the question is enormously important, that he is chewing on it himself, and that he hopes not.

item.title: Stocks and Bonds Are Actually Equally Risky, and Nobody Tells You
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-hiddenforces-股票和债券的风险其实一样大-只是没人告诉你/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-hiddenforces-股票和债券的风险其实一样大-只是没人告诉你/
item.description: Stretch the holding period to 20 years and the volatility of stocks and bonds is nearly identical — bonds are in fact more likely to post a real loss. So what long-term investors should really watch isn't a market benchmark, it's purchasing power.
item.content:encoded:
Stretch the holding period to 20 years and the volatility of stocks and bonds is nearly identical — bonds are in fact more likely to post a real loss. So what long-term investors should really watch isn't a market benchmark, it's purchasing power.

Medium information density. The first half lays out the philosophy; the real value is in the second half — the argument about how risk is defined, inflation as the benchmark, and the reversal in stock-bond correlation.

10:04 Recency bias has two layers, not just the post-1980 one
Inigo splits the recency bias investors need to strip away into two layers: one is the low inflation, high growth and negative stock-bond correlation since 1980; the other is longer — the US-led rules-based order after World War II. He argues neither regime applies in the same way now, so the question isn't ‘the future is uncertain’ — you could say that in any year — but what's left once you peel away both layers of experience. He names three sources of uncertainty that are genuinely different from the past: AI, climate change and geopolitical change.

21:26 Different holding periods care about fundamentally different things
Inigo rejects the idea that ‘the long term is just a string of short terms stitched together’. Within a year, technicals, momentum and flows matter most; approaching ten years, valuation and growth rates matter most; beyond that, preserving purchasing power becomes the core. He draws a specific dividing line: an investor with a rolling one-year horizon who wants to hedge inflation should buy assets positively correlated with inflation, such as commodities or TIPS; but a long-term investor shouldn't care about an asset's correlation to inflation, but about whether that asset can still generate a real return under persistently high and volatile inflation — and those aren't necessarily the same assets. Stocks and farmland could both make the cut.

30:44 Over a 20-year holding period, stocks and bonds have equal volatility
This is the hardest argument in the piece. Inigo says people are used to reducing risk to one year's return volatility, but stretch the holding period out and the relative volatility of stocks and bonds flips: measured over a 20-year holding period, stocks and bonds are basically equal; put another way, once you go beyond a few business cycles, bonds are more likely than stocks to suffer a real loss. From this he derives the conclusion that governance matters more than allocation — because the definition of risk itself has to be settled by the governance layer before you can even talk about allocation. In the same passage he notes that the success or failure of a cross-asset momentum strategy can be measured over a very short window, whereas a cross-asset value strategy is measured in years.

36:52 Fix spending first, then decide whether to hold liquidity
Inigo breaks liquidity into two things. The first is hard: any necessary annual spending must sit outside the structure, be fixed in advance, and must not drift upward in good years — changing it should require a formal review. The second is opportunistic: holding liquidity to buy the dip depends on whether you'll actually use it. If you're willing to buy individual assets when prices are badly dislocated, the money is worth it; if you only make decisions at the asset-class level, or you're not sure you'll pull the trigger at all, then that money is an opportunity cost that drags on the portfolio, and you should end up close to fully invested.

40:06 Tax planning is taking a bigger share of after-tax returns
Inigo offers a portfolio judgment: the coming decades will most likely bring lower returns, while government debt to GDP is at very high levels, so whatever politicians say today, tax rates will rise on some time scale. Stack those two together and it means that for taxable investors, tax planning will take a larger share of after-tax returns than in many past years. He also names inflation as the leading long-term destroyer of wealth, arguing that punitive tax regimes or social unrest, while severe at certain moments, are extremely hard to hedge.

42:08 There are dozens of times more indices than stocks, and that's absurd
Inigo rejects market benchmarks as the organising principle for a long-term portfolio. He gives a concrete comparison: the number of global equity indices is already in the millions, while there are only about 45,000 stocks in the world including small caps — sixty or seventy times more buckets than assets to put in them. He goes further: at the cross-asset level there is no natural default benchmark at all. 60-40 became the default only because it happened to perform well over the past forty or fifty years; there's no theoretical basis for it. His alternative is to treat inflation as an exogenous target line and weight assets in a more risk-based way.

47:22 Negative stock-bond correlation is the exception; positive is the norm
Inigo says the negative correlation between stock and bond returns before 2022 has been baked into people's thinking, but it was actually a product of the special period of the past twenty or thirty years. Look back over the preceding 200 years and stock-bond correlation was positive most of the time. He sees a shift to positive correlation as a return to normal, and as more consistent with a world that suffers inflation shocks — shocks that may come from climate, deglobalisation or debt monetisation, none of which are growth-driven. So the cross-asset correlations that have been so friendly to investors in recent years no longer have a reason to exist, and a different approach is required.

48:25 Build a portfolio that survives on multiple paths
Inigo repeatedly stresses that he doesn't want to just say ‘the future is always uncertain’, but to point out that AI, climate, geopolitics and the breakdown of the rules-based order have made the forecast paths for the future extremely divergent, while our ability to model policy and growth under those paths is poor. The response is to build a portfolio that is robust across several different paths — for instance, imagine a combination of temperatures rising more than two degrees, geopolitical change, and AI's effect on employment turning out unexpectedly. The tool he mentions is the total portfolio approach: no longer treating asset class as the primary dimension of risk, but allocating risk according to the more fundamental factors that drive the portfolio — though that requires major governance change, and large institutions can only move slowly and humbly.

item.title: America's 'Godfather of Socialism' Chose to Work Inside the Democratic Party, Not Build a Rival
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-throughline-美国-社会主义教父-的选择-向民主党内部妥协-而非揭竿另立/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-24-throughline-美国-社会主义教父-的选择-向民主党内部妥协-而非揭竿另立/
item.description: Harrington bet that working inside the Democratic Party to reshape it would beat building a socialist party outside it — even if that meant campaigning for a pro-Vietnam War candidate in 1968.
item.content:encoded:
Harrington bet that working inside the Democratic Party to reshape it would beat building a socialist party outside it — even if that meant campaigning for a pro-Vietnam War candidate in 1968.

From Catholic faith through the underground left of the McCarthy era to a seat at the White House table, one man's life traces the full tension of a century of strategic splits on the American left.

1:02 DSA grew from 6,000 to 120,000 members in six years
When Sanders declared himself a 'democratic socialist' at Georgetown in 2015, DSA had just 6,000 members with an average age over 60 — practically a retirees' club. What actually detonated its growth wasn't Sanders himself (he never joined DSA) but Trump's election: a wave of people engaging in politics for the first time felt mainstream Democrats weren't confrontational enough, and DSA became their outlet. Membership climbed to 120,000, making it the largest socialist organization in American left-wing history.

15:48 A papal encyclical shaped him before Marx did
Harrington grew up in a devout Catholic family, and what first shaped his politics wasn't Marx but a papal encyclical from the 1890s calling for attention to the working class and a softening of capitalism's harms. After leaving the Church, he threw himself into New York's left-wing circles, studying under Max Shachtman, who had grown disillusioned with the Soviet Union. Together they set the tone for 'democratic socialism': anti-authoritarian, anti-communist, and self-identified with the Western bloc. His famous line — 'you can't be a socialist and not love America' — also invited a rebuttal from critics: doesn't that amount to whitewashing America's history of imperialism?

22:03 The poverty survey was written for the middle class, not the poor
The Other America used census data to argue that America was far poorer than people assumed: Black workers earned only 58% of what white workers did, and once you added in Native Americans, Latinos, farmworkers, and the elderly, somewhere between a quarter and a third of the entire population fell below the poverty line. But Harrington wrote the book for the middle class, not the poor — he didn't buy the traditional Marxist path of the working class organizing itself to seize change. He believed real change would come from persuaded, politically well-placed elites.

27:19 A self-declared socialist sat in on White House policy meetings
After Kennedy's assassination, Johnson, who succeeded him, wanted to finish what Roosevelt had left undone. His team brought in Harrington — an openly declared socialist — for legislative consultations on anti-poverty budgets running into the hundreds of millions of dollars, which eventually produced the 1964 War on Poverty. The experience convinced Harrington that running candidates as a standalone socialist party was 'a dead end that had already been tried for a century,' and that the real path was 'realignment' — pulling Black voters into the Democratic Party while pushing segregationist Southern Democrats out.

32:29 He stayed quiet on Vietnam to keep his White House access
Martin Luther King Jr. privately called himself a democratic socialist too, and he and Harrington grew close — King once joked that he only realized he was poor after reading Harrington's book. But when King began publicly denouncing the Vietnam War in 1967, calling the U.S. the world's largest purveyor of violence, Harrington — who also opposed the war — chose not to speak out loudly, worried that doing so would cost him his influence within the Johnson administration. He later admitted that he'd muted his real position to preserve his access to the White House, and it weighed on his conscience for the rest of his life.

38:47 In 1968 he campaigned for a pro-war candidate
After King and Kennedy were both assassinated, antiwar students rallied behind McCarthy, but Harrington backed Johnson's vice president, Humphrey — a pro-war candidate — on the grounds that he had the best shot at blocking Nixon, the lesser of two evils. Maurice Isserman, then a 17-year-old student activist, found this unacceptable and, like many young people, branded Harrington a 'sellout.' SDS soon turned openly Marxist-Leninist, splitting from Harrington for good.

44:02 Founding DSA required settling an Israel-Palestine split first
In 1982, Harrington merged his organization with another group made up of New Left veterans to form DSA — a merger rare in the history of the left. Before it could happen, the two sides had to settle a disagreement: Harrington was a committed Zionist who could recite Israel's national anthem, had supported Israel in both the 1967 and 1973 wars, and held the Palestinians more responsible for the conflict, while members of the other group were more sympathetic to the Palestinians. In the end, both sides set the disagreement aside in order to focus on defeating Reagan first.

50:15 On Israel-Palestine, DSA has now moved past him
Harrington himself held the Palestinians more responsible for the conflict and favored a two-state solution; when DSA was founded in 1982, the members more sympathetic to the Palestinians set that disagreement aside to focus on defeating Reagan first. His biographer says DSA's official stance today no longer even admits 'liberal Zionists' as members — far more radical than Harrington himself. It's hard to imagine he'd endorse that line, but if he'd lived another forty years, he'd probably have kept changing his mind too.
